name: Felix Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three and lead a building-site crew putting up timber partitions and fitting them around the services. My trade certificate started me off, but the awkward junctions are what the younger carpenters ask me about. I use AI now and then to compare a cut list after someone else has tested it. I earn well for this trade; my partner and I have more than six months of expenses set aside, two schoolchildren and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a faster materials list saves the office some minutes, while our crew still builds the partition. An AI cut list cannot tell when a building wall has moved out of square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the skilled fitting and my good wage to continue. We have over six months of expenses saved and plenty of nearby construction firms, so a modest software change does not threaten home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting out partitions with the crew and check the first bay by hand. I would use the familiar list tool occasionally, only after comparing its quantities with the measured room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my work and our mortgage in this picture. It is an ordinary improvement to a small part of the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the drawing most often fail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Where a service pipe meets an old wall. The partition needs a careful cut there, and the planned dimension is only a starting point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put more savings aside because of this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No new saving plan follows from a small ordering change. We already have a strong cushion and the same paid fitting work.

say: I would **welcome** quicker lists but still measure the first partition bay.
I would **tell** the crew that a drawing cannot see every wall on site.
think: Our **paid** fitting work looks secure, with savings beyond six months.
I **use** AI only occasionally after testing it against the room.
do: **Keep** leading partition installation and checking first bays by hand.
**Compare** familiar AI cut list with measured building rooms.
feel: **Calm** about secure skilled work and household money.
S0.quote: An AI cut list cannot tell when a building wall has moved out of square.
fieldNote: **Felix** treats the tool as an occasional aid, never a substitute for site measurement.
**High** wages, substantial savings and many nearby jobs make a small ordering change feel safe.

steps.text: Keep leading and measuring building-site partitions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the office may buy and plan faster, while our hands still fit the awkward partition bays. I would try a new AI sequencing tool after another site shows fewer delivery gaps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can see management asking the same crew for more bays per paid day. That could reduce overtime, though my normal wage and our savings would keep the mortgage safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my crew and compare paid hours and delivered materials on two jobs. If the sequencing tool works on actual site records, I would learn its controls and ask the manager how the new targets affect pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about overtime possibly shrinking, but I have room to test the change. I would not assume the software itself decides our rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What result would persuade you to use the sequencing tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The timber needs to arrive before the crew starts that bay, with no unpaid waiting. A faster AI plan could turn my partition crew’s overtime into an unpaid target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you handle a smaller overtime cheque?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could cover the mortgage without overtime. I would still ask for the rate and targets in writing before accepting more bays for the same paid day.

say: I would **test** new AI sequencing against real deliveries and paid site time.
I would **ask** whether faster plans mean more partition bays for the same wage.
think: **Overtime** could shrink even if my basic wage and mortgage remain secure.
A **proven** tool is worth learning; management should state the targets.
do: **Compare** paid fitting hours and material arrivals on two partition jobs.
**Learn** AI sequencing controls only after a proven site test.
**Ask** builder for written partition targets and wage terms.
feel: **Anxious** about plausible overtime loss, with a strong cushion.
S1.quote: A faster AI plan could turn my partition crew’s overtime into an unpaid target.
fieldNote: He is **open** to a new tool after site proof and distinguishes a target decision from software capability.
**Possible** overtime loss is his own income risk, even though base pay and savings support the household.

steps.text: Keep paid partition work while comparing site records
Learn proven AI sequencing controls on actual partition jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI in 2028, when I am forty-five, can plan partitions but not fit them by hand. The capable site robots around 2031, when I am forty-eight, could take the straight bays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose paid fitting hours if robots do standard partitions, though the difficult junctions may keep a crew. Our savings and the many local builders give me choices, but they do not guarantee my current wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the builder for a safe paid trial measuring robot-built partitions and keep normal shifts while it runs. If robot work cuts my hours, I would apply to posted local fit-out lead jobs only if the wage covers the mortgage and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about possible hours loss, not overwhelmed. I have time, savings and local firms to approach if it happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes a robot-built partition safe to accept?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check fixing points and the gap around each service opening against the site specification. A robot can build a straight partition, but someone still has to sign for the fire-stopping around a real service pipe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept less money to leave before robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would keep the current good wage unless a posted local role offered enough for our household and a clear start date.

say: **Thinking** AI affects planning in 2028; robots may fit standard partition bays around 2031.
I would **insist** on safe checks during a paid robot trial.
think: My **paid** hours could shrink, though awkward fitting and nearby jobs give options.
A **move** requires a posted local role with wages that cover the mortgage and children.
do: **Request** paid site trial checking robot-built partition fixings and service gaps.
**Keep** normal paid fitting shifts during the trial.
**Apply** after lost hours to posted local fit-out lead role at household-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about possible paid-hour cuts, with savings and local alternatives.
S2.quote: A robot can build a straight partition, but someone still has to sign for the fire-stopping around a real service pipe.
fieldNote: His **proposed** trial includes a concrete safety check and paid time, rather than a vague interest in robots.
He **separates** 2028 planning from 2031 hands-on work and would apply only for real adequate local roles.

steps.text: Keep normal paid partition shifts if requested safe robot trial runs
Apply after hour cuts to posted local fit-out lead job with adequate pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2031 thinking AI changes the office work when I am forty-eight, and hands-on robots follow around 2034 when I am fifty-one. The extra years let us see a real inspection role before I change trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a site safety inspection course if the builder funds it, pays my training days and shows a posted local vacancy. A fire-stopping certificate is useful when a local builder has a paid inspection place for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the partition crew and enroll in a funded, paid-time inspection course only if a suitable local opening is posted. After qualifying, I would apply to that posted job only if its wage covers mortgage and school costs; I would check robot-built fire-stopping against the site specification.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about later robots and somewhat anxious if standard bays lose paid hours. The longer lead time lets me verify both training and employment terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which inspection would you learn to sign for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fire-stopping around pipes where partitions meet floors and ceilings. A formal course would cover the record and responsibility beyond my current fitting checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the vacancy exists but training time is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the current paid crew role and ask another builder about paid training. High savings give me choices, but I will not buy a speculative title.

say: The 2031 **planning** change comes before robots handle site fitting around 2034.
I would **train** for fire-stopping inspection with funded paid time and a posted local opening.
think: A **real** vacancy and adequate wage matter more than an attractive certificate.
My **current** partition checks are not the same as formal inspection sign-off.
do: **Enroll** in funded paid-time fire-stopping course for posted suitable local role.
**Keep** paid partition work until inspection offer exists.
**Apply** after qualification to posted local inspection job at household-covering wage.
feel: **Anxious** about possible standard-bay cuts, with time to check terms.
S3.quote: A fire-stopping certificate is useful when a local builder has a paid inspection place for it.
fieldNote: He would **actually** enroll only after full funding, paid time and a posted suitable local role align.
The **application** after qualifying preserves the local wage requirement and physical safety duty.

steps.text: Enroll in funded paid-time fire-stopping course for posted local role
Keep paid partition shifts until inspection offer
Apply after qualification to posted local inspector job at adequate wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI comes in 2036 when I am fifty-three, with capable hands-on robots around 2039 when I am fifty-six. A ten-year robot forecast will not make me leave a well-paid partition crew for an unposted job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would expect several more years of good paid partition work. Our savings already cover over six months, and plenty of local builders exist, so I need not rush into a course that may lead nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading site partitions and add new money from my higher wages to the mortgage reserve each quarter after bills. If a funded course on paid time and a posted adequate local inspection role appear, I would complete the training and apply after qualifying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next few years and uneasy about the distant robot date. The long warning makes careful saving and job checks possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why add to savings when you already have a strong cushion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot timetable can change, but each new transfer from wages also reduces pressure on the mortgage. I would not count existing cash twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change jobs just because the robots are forecast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would wait for a posted local inspection job with adequate pay and funded paid training before leaving a well-paid crew.

say: I would **keep** skilled fitting work and add fresh wages to our reserve.
I would **wait** for a posted adequate local inspection role before funded training.
think: **Strong** savings and many local jobs make the long transition manageable.
A **certificate** without a funded paid course and actual vacancy is unnecessary now.
do: **Keep** leading paid partition fitting while checking real robot results.
**Save** new wages quarterly after mortgage and school bills.
**Complete** funded paid-time course for posted adequate local inspection job.
feel: **Calm** about present work, uneasy about distant robots.
S4.quote: A ten-year robot forecast will not make me leave a well-paid partition crew for an unposted job.
fieldNote: His **long** plan preserves well-paid work, adds new wage savings and waits for evidence from real buildings.
**Any** later course and application remain conditional on funding, paid time, a posted local opening and adequate wages.

steps.text: Save new wages quarterly after household bills
Complete funded paid-time course for posted adequate local inspection job
Apply after qualification to posted local inspection role with household-covering pay

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028/2031 case worries me most because standard partition hours might shrink. A paid safety trial, honest hours plan and posted nearby inspection or fit-out job at adequate wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs the fire-stopping after a robot fits a wall. The new machine may be quick, but the safety duty still sits in a real building. My tape measure can travel to another builder; my mortgage cannot live on a promised vacancy.

headlineQuote: My tape measure can travel to another builder; my mortgage cannot live on a promised vacancy.
portrait: **Felix** is a forty-three-year-old trade-certified lead carpenter who fits building-site partitions.
His **higher** pay, savings beyond six months, mortgage, schoolchildren and plentiful nearby jobs give him options.
He **uses** AI occasionally after proof on site and requires a paid safety trial for robot-built work.
**Training** and applications require funding, paid time, posted local work and wages covering the household.
biggestWorry: **Fast** robots around 2031 could cut paid standard partition hours, despite his strong savings and local alternatives.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid** safety trial, clear hours and a posted local role at household-covering pay would help.
